interviewQuestions.question: A single-page app's memory usage grows steadily the longer a user stays on the page, and a heap snapshot shows a rising count of detached DOM nodes. What's happening, and how do you find and fix the cause?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A detached DOM node is one that's been removed from the visible document but is still **reachable** from JavaScript — something in the code still holds a reference to it, so the garbage collector can't reclaim it even though the page no longer shows it.

How I'd find it: take two heap snapshots in Chrome DevTools while repeating whatever action removes the elements (closing a modal, navigating away from a list), and use the Comparison view filtered to "Detached" — the count growing by roughly one per repetition is the leak signature. Clicking into a specific detached node and reading its **Retainers** panel shows the actual chain of references keeping it alive.

The usual root cause is one of a few shapes: a cache or lookup map keyed by DOM element that's never cleaned up when the element is removed; a closure captured by an event listener attached to something outside the removed subtree (so removing the subtree doesn't remove the listener); or a framework ref/handle held in component state that outlives the actual DOM removal.

The fix is always the same idea: whatever code removes the element from the page also needs to drop every other reference to it — delete the cache entry, call `removeEventListener` with the same function reference that was added, and null out any stored ref. The node then has zero reachable paths and gets collected on the next pass.

**Testing:** whether you can turn "detached DOM nodes" from a term you've heard into an actual diagnostic and fix workflow.

interviewQuestions.question: How does JavaScript's garbage collector decide what to free, and why doesn't a reference cycle between two objects cause a leak the way it might in a naive reference-counting system?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The collector works from **reachability**, not reference counting. Starting from a set of roots — global variables, and every variable frame currently on the call stack — it walks every reference it can follow and marks every object it reaches. Anything left unmarked after that walk is provably inaccessible from any running code and gets swept, its memory reclaimed.

That's exactly why a reference cycle isn't a special case here: two objects pointing at each other, with **no path from any root** to either one, simply never get marked in the first place. The mark phase starts from roots and follows outward — it never even considers the cycle unless something reachable points into it. Contrast this with a naive reference-counting scheme (each object tracks how many things point to it, freed when the count hits zero): two objects referencing only each other would keep each other's count at one forever, leaking indefinitely, since nothing external ever decrements it. Some older systems and some non-cyclic-aware collectors genuinely have this weakness; JavaScript's mark-and-sweep design sidesteps it structurally.

Where JavaScript engines still layer in something count-like is for performance, not correctness — generational collection (young vs old generation, in V8's case) is an optimization on top of the same reachability idea, exploiting the fact that most objects die young, not a different correctness model.

**Testing:** whether you understand mark-and-sweep as reachability from roots, specifically well enough to explain why it doesn't share reference-counting's classic cycle weakness.

interviewQuestions.question: You're building a cache that maps DOM elements to computed layout data, refreshed on scroll. Would you use a `Map` or a `WeakMap`, and why does it matter here specifically?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
`WeakMap`, and the reason is directly about element lifetime: elements get added and removed from the DOM constantly as the user scrolls (virtualized lists, infinite scroll, conditionally rendered sections), and a regular `Map` would keep every element that was ever cached alive **forever**, because a `Map`'s keys are strong references — the map itself is enough to keep an entry's key reachable, independent of whether the element is still in the document.

With a `WeakMap`, once an element has no other references — removed from the DOM, and nothing else in the app still points to it — it becomes eligible for garbage collection, and its entry in the `WeakMap` disappears along with it automatically. There's no manual cleanup code needed for the cache side of things at all; the cache never grows unbounded even though it's never explicitly pruned.

What I'd watch for: `WeakMap` doesn't support iteration (`.keys()`, `.forEach()`) or a `.size` property, precisely because its contents can shrink at any moment via garbage collection outside your control — so it's the wrong choice if the code ever needs to enumerate everything currently cached, not just look up by a specific element. In that case I'd combine a bounded regular `Map` (with explicit LRU-style eviction) instead, trading automatic cleanup for the ability to inspect the whole cache.

**Testing:** whether you can justify `WeakMap` from the actual lifetime problem it solves, not just recall that it exists.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Design trade-offs

interviewQuestions.question: A hot code path creates thousands of small temporary objects per second (e.g., mapping over a large array on every render). Is this a memory problem you should optimize away?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Usually no — and understanding why requires knowing how V8 (and similar engines) actually run garbage collection, not just "GC handles it."

Engines exploit the observation that **most objects die young**: a short-lived object created and discarded within a function call is the overwhelmingly common case. V8 splits the heap into a small, frequently-collected **young generation** and a larger, less-often-collected **old generation**; an object surviving a couple of young-generation collections gets promoted. The young-generation collector (a "scavenge") is specifically tuned to be cheap for exactly this churn pattern — creating and discarding thousands of small objects per second in a hot loop is close to the ideal case it was designed for, not a pathological one.

The actual performance risk isn't object creation volume — it's objects that **should** be short-lived getting accidentally retained long enough to reach the old generation, because the old-generation collector is a heavier mark-and-sweep-and-compact pass. That happens when a hot-path object gets captured by a closure, pushed into a long-lived array, or stashed in a cache that never evicts.

So my answer in an interview: I wouldn't pre-optimize away short-lived object creation on the strength of "garbage collection is expensive" — I'd profile first (Chrome's Performance panel shows GC pause time directly), and only chase it if GC time is actually showing up as a measurable chunk of frame budget. If it is, the fix is almost always object pooling or reusing a buffer, not simply "create fewer objects" as a blanket rule.

**Testing:** whether you understand generational GC well enough to push back on a plausible-sounding but usually-wrong optimization instinct.
